title: 330 players stayed 30+ seconds in my FPS. Only 29 reached a score. How would you debug this with AI?
author: Ilya_Kra
selftext:
Something surprised me while testing my browser FPS, FRONTBREAK.

Over 90 days, the game had 548 page visits and 427 launches. Of those, 330 made it past 30 seconds, but only 29 triggered a score event.

That's a 91% gap.

I've been experimenting with AI-assisted QA using MCP tools. An AI agent can interact with the game in a browser, send keyboard/mouse inputs, inspect screenshots and game state, and help investigate problems.

I'm also comparing gameplay events with opt-in tester recordings to understand what actually happens.

My current suspicion is that players don't get enough score/progress feedback during a round. But the tracking itself could also be wrong.

Next, I want to validate the score event, review recordings, try clearer in-game feedback, and measure the difference.

AI can suggest fixes, but I still need real gameplay data to know whether they actually work.

**Have you tried using AI to debug player behavior rather than just code? What would you investigate first?**

I'm the developer of the game and its testing workflow. Sharing the findings to get technical feedback, not promoting a service.

comments.author: maxneuds
comments.body:
Fixing a game that is not interesting to play is not debugging. That means your concept is not interesting. And here is the thing: AI will not fix that for you because AI is a statistical model and it's really bad at being creative and inventing something new that has no score to test against. "Make my game fun to play" what will this trigger? It will make the most likely game players reviewed as fun on the internet meaning the most average and generic game you can image which is absolutely not fun.

If you want to create a game that people actually play, especially with bad graphics, then you need to come up with a unique and creative idea that's fun to play or even addicting to play. And the millionths FPS or the 1000s FPS shoulder that was thrown into the internet just that day alone by AI will definitely not do the trick. You can be happy that even someone launched the game.

I just took a look at it and it's the most generic shit I have seen in a long time. Looks like Temu Counter Strike and even intuitive crouching doesn't exist. It reminds me of these truckloads of bad Flash Games from the early 2000s which also surprised me why these even exist if actual good games exist that cost next to nothing.

replies.author: Ilya_Kra
replies.body: I get your point, but I'm not asking AI to make this game fun 😅 FRONTBREAK is just an example. I'm building a gaming platform where devs can share a test link and see how real people play, where they click and why they might leave. That's what I'm testing here.

comments.author: EinArchitekt
comments.body:
Measure your funnel. Do you have tutorial? Measure where players quit. Do you provide frictionless signup or require an account? Where did your players come from, ai/dev-spaces? Real player audience?

I would setup funnel measurement including origin of visitors and figure out where players leave first. Divide by mobile / desktop users so you can better answer the question depending on device.

comments.author: bluesmaker
comments.body:
From googling, "FRONTBREAK is a free online FPS built around a 5v5 bomb mode, with a buy phase before every round and five maps to learn. It runs in your browser on a computer or phone, with bots or real players."

So this is a heavily counter-strike inspired game. Even looking at the map you include in the image, I can see it's that A,B, mid type map that's used in all CS.

What makes CS fun? The PvP. Playing against bots isn't great. They are excellent for filling empty slots, but if it's just you and bots, that's not fun. You say over 90 days you had 427 launches. So it would be fair to assume few (perhaps even none) of those players actually were in the game while another player was. That seems to be your problem. 

Here's another problem: is having the game work in a browser really a selling point? Counter-Strike 2 is free to play. Not trying to be harsh, but how can you hope to attract players when they can just have the real thing? What makes this better? How can you communicate what this game offers to potential players?

Really, I think you need to take some serious deviations from CS, such that you can describe the game without sounding like an imitation of the real thing. 

Again, not wanting to be harsh, but it's a little surprising how you seem puzzled by the state of things.

replies.author: Ilya_Kra
replies.body: Yeah, I get what you mean. FRONTBREAK is one of my own games, and I picked it specifically because it's 3D. I wanted to see how well my recording tool handles actual 3D gameplay. I'm testing the tool here, not trying to compete with CS2 😅

replies.author: Leggerity
replies.body: Right, and they're explaining people are getting bored with your game because it's a CS2 clone with no PVP. Boredom is why you're seeing those numbers. Players do not want to see it through.
